section_heading: 1.1 Clinical Presentation and Chest Pain Characteristics
text: Chest pain should be considered as pain, pressure, tightness, or discomfort in the chest, neck, shoulders, jaw, or arms. The term "atypical" chest pain is discouraged as it is misleading; instead, pain should be described as cardiac, possibly cardiac, or noncardiac. Features suggestive of acute coronary syndrome (ACS) include retrosternal pain radiating to the left arm, neck, or jaw, associated with diaphoresis, dyspnea, nausea, and lightheadedness. Features decreasing the likelihood of acute myocardial ischemia include sharp, pleuritic chest pain aggravated by respiration, strictly localized with one finger, or reproduced by chest wall palpation.

A 12-lead ECG must be performed and evaluated within 10 minutes of patient arrival in all patients presenting with acute chest pain. ST-elevation indicates immediate STEMI pathway activation and urgent reperfusion. ST-segment depression (especially horizontal or downsloping >= 0.5 mm) or deep symmetrical T-wave inversions strongly suggest high-risk acute ischemia or non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI). Chest radiography (Chest X-Ray) is recommended for all patients with acute chest pain to assess for alternative or concomitant conditions, including: 1. Cardiomegaly and pulmonary venous congestion (suggesting congestive heart failure). 2. Pneumonia or pulmonary consolidation. 3. Pneumothorax (absence of peripheral lung markings). 4. Widened mediastinum (suggesting thoracic aortic dissection requiring urgent CTA).

High-sensitivity cardiac troponin (hs-cTn I or T) is the preferred biomarker for detecting myocardial injury. Serial sampling protocols (0/1-hour, 0/2-hour, or 0/3-hour) are recommended to assess for significant dynamic delta rises. In patients with low clinical risk scores and undetectable baseline hs-cTn levels, early discharge and outpatient management are safe. In patients with intermediate or high clinical risk, elevated baseline troponin, or significant dynamic rise, hospitalization and inpatient cardiology consultation are indicated.

For patients presenting with acute chest pain, validated clinical risk scores (such as HEART Score or EDACS) should be utilized. The HEART Score evaluates: - History (Slightly, Moderately, or Highly suspicious) - ECG (Normal, Non-specific repolarization disturbance, or Significant ST deviation) - Age (<45, 45-64, >=65) - Risk Factors (Hypertension, Hypercholesterolemia, Diabetes, Smoking, Family History, Obesity) - Troponin (<= normal limit, 1-3x normal limit, >3x normal limit) A low HEART score (0-3) identifies patients with <2% 30-day major adverse cardiac event (MACE) risk suitable for outpatient disposition. A score of 4-6 indicates intermediate risk requiring observation and provocative or anatomical testing (CCTA or Stress SPECT/MRI). A score of 7-10 represents high risk requiring direct coronary angiography and aggressive anti-ischemic medical therapy.

section_heading: 2.1 Universal Definition and Classification of Heart Failure
text: Heart failure is a complex clinical syndrome with symptoms and signs resulting from structural or functional cardiac abnormality. Classification by Left Ventricular Ejection Fraction (LVEF): 1. Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF): LVEF <= 40%. 2. Heart Failure with Mildly Reduced Ejection Fraction (HFmrEF): LVEF 41% to 49%. 3. Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction (HFpEF): LVEF >= 50% with evidence of elevated filling pressures. 4. Heart Failure with Improved Ejection Fraction (HFimpEF): Baseline LVEF <= 40% with a >= 10-point increase to > 40%.

section_heading: 2.2 Diagnostic Evaluation and Medical Imaging in Heart Failure
text: 1. Laboratory evaluation: - Serum B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) or N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) is strongly recommended (Class 1) to support diagnosis or exclude HF. Elevated levels correlate with hemodynamic wall stress. - Complete blood count, serum creatinine, electrolytes, fasting glucose, lipid profile, liver function tests, and thyroid stimulating hormone. 2. Chest Radiography (CXR): - Recommended in initial evaluation to detect cardiomegaly (cardiothoracic ratio > 0.50), pulmonary venous congestion, interstitial/alveolar pulmonary edema (Kerley B lines), and bilateral pleural effusions. - Distinguishes primary pulmonary disease from cardiogenic decompensation. 3. Transthoracic Echocardiogram (TTE): - Mandatory initial imaging modality to determine LVEF, chamber sizes, ventricular wall thickness, diastolic function, and valvular abnormalities.

In all patients with HFrEF (Stage C), the foundational 4-pillar medical therapy is recommended to reduce hospitalizations and all-cause mortality: 1. Renin-Angiotensin System Inhibition: - Angiotensin Receptor-Neprilysin Inhibitor (ARNI, sacubitril/valsartan) is preferred first-line over ACE inhibitors or ARBs. - In patients who cannot tolerate ARNI, ACE inhibitors (enalapril, lisinopril, ramipril) or ARBs (candesartan, valsartan) are indicated. 2. Evidence-Based Beta-Blockers: - One of three proven beta-blockers: Carvedilol, Metoprolol Succinate extended-release, or Bisoprolol. 3. Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists (MRA): - Spironolactone or Eplerenone in patients with eGFR > 30 mL/min/1.73m2 and serum potassium < 5.0 mEq/L. 4. Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) Inhibitors: - Empagliflozin (10 mg daily) or Dapagliflozin (10 mg daily), regardless of diabetes status. Loop diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide, torsemide) should be titrated to achieve and maintain euvolemia.

section_heading: 2.4 Prevention of Decompensation and Inpatient Escalation
text: Patients with resting systolic BP < 90 mm Hg, worsening renal function (creatinine rise > 0.5 mg/dL), intractable peripheral edema, or rest dyspnea require urgent hospital admission. Evaluation of secondary precipitating causes: medication non-adherence, dietary sodium indiscretion, concurrent respiratory infection, acute myocardial ischemia, or unmanaged tachyarrhythmias (atrial fibrillation).

document_title: Ats Idsa Community Acquired Pneumonia Guidelines
text: A clinical diagnosis of Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP) requires: 1. Symptoms of acute lower respiratory tract infection (cough, fever, dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, sputum production, auscultatory crackles/bronchial breath sounds). 2. Radiographic confirmation: Chest radiography (CXR) showing the presence of a new or progressive pulmonary infiltrate, consolidation, or air bronchograms. CXR is vital to differentiate pneumonia from acute bronchitis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbation, and congestive heart failure. CT of the chest is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty, immunocompromised hosts, or suspicion of complications (empyema, cavitation, abscess, underlying malignancy).

section_heading: 3.2 Site-of-Care Decisions and Severity Scores (CURB-65 / PSI)
text: Clinicians should use a validated clinical prediction rule for prognosis, preferably the Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI), supplemented by CURB-65 criteria. CURB-65 Criteria (1 point for each present): - Confusion (new onset disorientation) - Urea (BUN > 19 mg/dL or > 7 mmol/L) - Respiratory rate >= 30 breaths/min - Blood pressure (Systolic BP < 90 mm Hg or Diastolic BP <= 60 mm Hg) - Age >= 65 years Triage recommendations: - Score 0 to 1: Low risk (<3% 30-day mortality); outpatient treatment is recommended. - Score 2: Intermediate risk (approx. 9% mortality); inpatient hospital admission or closely monitored outpatient observation. - Score 3 to 5: High risk (15-40% mortality); inpatient admission, evaluate for intensive care unit (ICU) admission if severe criteria met.

document_title: Ats Idsa Community Acquired Pneumonia Guidelines
text: 1. For outpatients without comorbidities or risk factors for antibiotic-resistant pathogens: - Amoxicillin 1 g orally 3 times daily (strong recommendation), OR - Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily (conditional recommendation), OR - Macrolide (azithromycin 500 mg on day 1, then 250 mg daily; or clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily) ONLY in areas with pneumococcal macrolide resistance < 25%. 2. For outpatients with comorbidities (chronic heart failure, COPD, diabetes, renal failure, liver disease, malignancy, asplenia): - Combination therapy: Beta-lactam (Amoxicillin/clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily or 2000/125 mg twice daily; or Cefuroxime 500 mg twice daily) PLUS a Macrolide (Azithromycin) or Doxycycline, OR - Monotherapy with a respiratory fluoroquinolone (Levofloxacin 750 mg daily, or Moxifloxacin 400 mg daily).

document_title: Ats Idsa Community Acquired Pneumonia Guidelines
text: 1. Nonsevere Inpatient CAP: - Standard regimen: Beta-lactam (Ampicillin/sulbactam 1.5-3 g every 6h, Cefotaxime 1-2 g every 8h, or Ceftriaxone 1-2 g daily) PLUS a macrolide (Azithromycin 500 mg daily IV/oral), OR - Monotherapy with a respiratory fluoroquinolone (Levofloxacin 750 mg daily IV/oral). 2. Corticosteroids: Routine use of systemic corticosteroids is NOT recommended in patients with nonsevere CAP. Corticosteroids are reserved for refractory septic shock or concomitant COPD/asthma exacerbation. Duration of therapy: Minimum of 5 days, continuing until clinical stability is achieved (afebrile for 48 hours and no more than 1 sign of clinical instability).
